## B.2 The lessons-learned claim, and why it is a cost-attribution problem

HII's own framing is the single most useful sentence in the public record for a cost model, because it asserts that the second-ship learning benefit did not land:

> "Specifically, *John F. Kennedy* (CVN 79) construction was fairly advanced when many *Ford* lessons were realized, precluding timely implementation of lessons learned for *Kennedy*. In contrast, *Enterprise* (CVN 80) and *Doris Miller* (CVN 81) have been able to incorporate, leverage and capitalize on *Ford* lessons learned earlier in the construction process."
> Todd Corillo, NNS spokesperson, quoted in [USNI 7 Jul 2025](https://news.usni.org/2025/07/07/carrier-john-f-kennedy-delivery-delayed-2-years-fleet-will-drop-to-10-carriers-for-1-year)

**The 11-carrier floor.** 10 U.S.C. 8062(b) requires not less than 11 operational aircraft carriers. The DON Financial Management Policy Manual states that SCN is **line item appropriated**, unlike every other DON appropriation, and that the SCN four-digit subhead encodes the budget activity and P-1 line:

The DON Financial Management Policy Manual states that SCN is **line item appropriated**, unlike every other DON appropriation, and that the SCN four-digit subhead encodes the budget activity and P-1 line:

> "The Shipbuilding and Conversion, Navy (SCN) appropriation is divided into five budget activities... further divided into procurement line items (P-1 line item) for which funds have been budgeted... activity and P-1 line each represents one of the four positions of the subhead for this appropriation."

Sources: [DON FMPM](https://www.secnav.navy.mil/fmc/Documents/FINAL-FMPM.pdf), mirrored copy that renders in search: https://www.navymwr.org/modules/media/?do=download&id=db495ee9-737a-4399-8751-d21cda75ebf3 and https://www.secnav.navy.mil/fmc/Documents/Financial-Management-Policy.pdf

721d39f9237e6944:0003:14.text:
-FMPM.pdf), mirrored copy that renders in search: https://www.navymwr.org/modules/media/?do=download&id=db495ee9-737a-4399-8751-d21cda75ebf3 and https://www.secnav.navy.mil/fmc/Documents/Financial-Management-Policy.pdf

**Why this is the key:** because SCN is line-item appropriated and the subhead carries BA plus P-1 line, the subhead in the ledger is a direct, structural pointer to the Carrier Replacement Program. In Navy ERP the subhead is mapped to the NWA or WBS. Confirmed in the DTS/LOA data dictionary: "ACCT 3 - Subhead with the NAVY ERP subhead table for the NWA or WBS." [DTA Appendix R](https://media.defense.gov/2021/Nov/15/2002893225/-1/-1/0/DTA_APP_R.PDF), [LOA formats by service](https://acqnotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/09/Lines-of-Accounting-LOAS-Formats-by-Service-Agency-and-LOA-Data-Elements-For-Customer-Identification-Codes-CICS.pdf)

- Estimate classes A through F. **Class C is the recommended classification for budget submittals to Congress, NAVCOMPT, and higher authority.** Class F is a feasibility "ball park" estimate from a one-digit SWBS weight group.

**OWLD, the cost-scope boundary that matters most.**
- GAO: OWLD is "the date when full financial responsibility for maintaining and operating" the ship transfers. "All new work identified after OWLD is the fleet's responsibility to correct using non-construction funding accounts, per Navy policy." GAO treats OWLD as the date the ship is provided to the fleet. [GAO-17-418](https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-17-418.pdf)
- **OPNAVINST 4700.8M:** "The CFO date becomes the basis for establishing the OWLD, which is **11 months following the CFO** of the ship." PSA is normally complete one to two months prior to OWLD. Obligations for construction, conversion, outfitting, and post-delivery must occur prior to OWLD. https://www.secnav.navy.mil/doni/Directives/04000%20Logistical%20Support%20and%20Services/04-700%20General%20Maintenance%20and%20Construction%20Support/4700.8M.pdf
- **NAVSEA Desk Reference for SCN:** "The overall OWLD for SCN funding is **thirteen months after delivery** of the ship." Also: SEA 01P "has consistently ruled to permit work after the work-limiting date, but within the" scope planned in good faith before it. http://pdf4pro.com/cdn/scn-desk-reference-sunset-design-5526fa.pdf

Asset valuation and evaluation

## I.1 Is Kennedy on the Navy's books? Yes, but not as a ship.

As of today the hull sits in **Construction in Progress**, not in Vessels. The accounting is explicit about the mechanism.
721d39f9237e6944:0007:07.heading: I

721d39f9237e6944:0007:08.text:
n Vessels. The accounting is explicit about the mechanism.

- **SFFAS 6** requires that for constructed PP&E, cost be accumulated in a CIP account and transferred to the applicable General PP&E account when construction is complete and the asset is placed in service. [FASAB standards](https://fasab.gov/accounting-standards/document-by-chapter/)
- **FMR Volume 4, Chapter 25** (which supersedes the long-cited Chapter 6) sets out the lifecycle. A CIP account is created after the decision to proceed is granted at Milestone C and the funding authorization document is complete (section 2.4.7.4). "Upon the date the asset is placed in service, the CIP will be relieved by the funding entity" (2.4.3.1). "When constructed items are accepted, the costs accumulated in the CIP account must be relieved" (2.4.7.8). Contractor Acquired Property "must be recognized by the funding DoD Component as general equipment when the item is delivered and accepted," and until acceptance, constructive delivery is recorded in CIP (2.4.1.6). https://comptroller.defense.gov/Portals/45/documents/fmr/current/04/04_25.pdf
- The **Military Equipment Valuation CAP business rule** states the same thing from the title side: title passes to DoD when the contractor obtains the property, but the property is not recorded on DoD financial statements "as other than construction in process" until it is delivered to DoD.

721d39f9237e6944:0007:09.text:
thing from the title side: title passes to DoD when the contractor obtains the property, but the property is not recorded on DoD financial statements "as other than construction in process" until it is delivered to DoD. https://www.acq.osd.mil/asda/dpc/ke/gfp/docs/MEV-Contractor-Acquired-Property-Business-Rule.pdf

**The live question this creates for CVN-79.** The ship reached **preliminary acceptance on 29 September 2026** and is scheduled for **delivery in March 2027**. Chapter 25 ties CIP relief to "placed in service" in one sentence and to "accepted" in another. Preliminary acceptance is an acceptance event that is explicitly not delivery. ## I.3 The three structural reasons capitalized value will never equal program cost

This is the part worth briefing, because it is not a data quality problem. It is definitional, and it will not go away with better data.
721d39f9237e6944:0007:20.heading: I

721d39f9237e6944:0008:00.text:
1. **Scope.** Capitalized value is the acquisition cost of the asset placed in service. Program cost includes things that never capitalize: terminated or reworked scope, the cost of delay, class research that benefited later hulls, government program office overhead, and FMS-funded content. Separately, the **$1 million Navy threshold means every component below it is expensed rather than capitalized even though it is physically installed on the ship**. Magnitude of that expensed tail for this hull is unknown and is **G19**.
2. **Timing.** Program cost accrues from FY2001 or FY2007 depending on the convention. Capitalized value appears at a single instant at placed in service. Roughly twenty years of accumulated cost collapses onto one date, and the depreciation clock then runs 50 years forward from it. No single report shows both shapes.
3. **Boundary.** Two different authorities set two different end points. **OWLD** governs what may be charged to the appropriation and is 11 months after completion of fitting out or 13 months after delivery depending on which document you read (E-3). **Placed in service** governs when the asset is recognized. They are different dates, set by different offices, for different purposes, and work legitimately charged to SCN after the asset is capitalized is real.

E-3). **Placed in service** governs when the asset is recognized. They are different dates, set by different offices, for different purposes, and work legitimately charged to SCN after the asset is capitalized is real.

A fourth divergence is a genuine open risk rather than a definitional one: **whether GFE installed on the hull is capitalized separately as its own general equipment or rolled into the vessel's value.** The EMALS and AAG shipsets, the eleven Advanced Weapons Elevators and the EASR array are each individually well above the $1 million threshold and each is procured on a different contract by a different command. If both the hull record and the system record capitalize them, the Navy double counts. If neither does, they drop. Registered as **G15**.

## K.3 The analytic point: that single number is five different things

A product that draws one line labeled "cost growth" will be wrong about four fifths of it. The public record supports at least five distinct mechanisms, and they belong in separate cause categories in the variance ledger:
721d39f9237e6944:0009:01.heading: K

721d39f9237e6944:0009:02.text: roduct that draws one line labeled "cost growth" will be wrong about four fifths of it. The public record supports at least five distinct mechanisms, and they belong in separate cause categories in the variance ledger:

721d39f9237e6944:0009:03.text:
elong in separate cause categories in the variance ledger:

1. **Estimate revision with no scope change.** FY2011 through FY2013 and FY2019. The ship did not change; the estimate did.
2. **Statute moving and the estimate following it.** FY2016 NDAA lowered the cap to $11,398.0M and the FY2017 submission estimated exactly $11,398.0M. This is the documented instance of GAO's finding that "rather than the program cost estimate informing the cost cap, the cost cap informed the program cost estimate."
3. **Genuine contract overrun.** August 2021, +$1.3 billion, attributed by the Navy to contract overruns at over 88% complete. This is the only one of the five that is cost growth in the ordinary sense.
4. **Scope transferred into the baseline.** The 2020 two-phase to single-phase delivery change and the 2023 move of Post Shakedown Availability work into the construction contract. Work the Navy was always going to pay for moved from one accounting period and account into another. The ship got more expensive; the program did not.
5. **Reclassification inside the program.** FY2026 to FY2027. GAO's own words: unit costs rose about $480 million, about half from delivery schedule changes, "but the Navy is using funds it previously planned and budgeted for post-delivery activities, **so these are not new program costs**."

- **Monopoly position.** The only US shipyard able to build large-deck nuclear carriers. Every US carrier procured since FY1958 was built there. The 2019 industrial base included roughly 2,000 supplier firms in 46 states. [CRS RS20643](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/RS/PDF/RS20643/RS20643.297.pdf)
- **Method: modular construction.** Smaller sections are welded into large structural units called **superlifts**, equipment is installed while the unit is still on the ground, and the unit is lifted into **Dry Dock 12** by a **1,050-metric-ton gantry crane**. [Marine Log](https://www.marinelog.com/shipbuilding/shipyards/shipyard-news/video-newport-news-carries-out-704-ton-superlift/)
- **Scale: CVN-79 was planned at 447 total lifts** (one NAVSEA briefing says 448). 317 erected by February 2018. 90% erected March 2019. The MSAR records the structural milestones against **447 total erectables**: 50% at 224 units (June 2017), 75% at 341 units (April 2018).

# PART N. Analyst reconstruction: how the hull total is made up

**This Part was rebuilt 2026-11-08 on primary documents.** An earlier version of it reasoned from estimates because the primary sources had not been pulled. # Background: domain reference

Facts about how carrier money moves and who states what about it, with sources. This is the
reference substrate so `BLUEPRINT.md` can reason without re-explaining the domain, and so `LOG.md`
can record decisions without restating the facts behind them. Items needing confirmation are marked
rather than asserted, and the open ones are tracked as gaps in `LOG.md`.

## 1. How appropriated money becomes a ship

Carrier cost does not arrive on one line in one year. It arrives through several appropriations
across more than a decade, and that structure produces most of the disagreements the system has to
explain.

**Research and development.** Ford-class design was funded through RDT&E. This is a class cost, not
attributable to a single hull by any direct method, which makes every hull-level figure that
includes an R&D share dependent on an allocation choice.

**Advance procurement.** Long-lead items, principally nuclear propulsion components, are
appropriated years before the fiscal year associated with the ship itself. A hull's cost therefore
begins accumulating in appropriation years before the year the hull is commonly said to belong to.

appropriated years before the fiscal year associated with the ship itself. A hull's cost therefore
begins accumulating in appropriation years before the year the hull is commonly said to belong to.

**Shipbuilding and Conversion, Navy (SCN).** The construction appropriation, and a multiple-year
appropriation, so obligation availability extends past the year of enactment. Each fiscal year's SCN
appropriation is separate and discrete. Ships are a recognized exception to full funding policy, so
a carrier is funded incrementally across several fiscal years. There is no single year in which the
ship was bought, and the figure a document reports depends on whether it describes one year's
increment, the cumulative appropriation to date, or the total estimated cost at completion. SCN is
divided into budget activities, and its four-digit subhead structure carries the identifying data
elements.

**Other procurement and related lines.** Government-furnished equipment arrives through separate
lines. Whether any of it counts as part of the ship's cost is a scope question with no universal
answer.

**Other procurement and related lines.** Government-furnished equipment arrives through separate
lines. Whether any of it counts as part of the ship's cost is a scope question with no universal

**Outfitting, post-delivery, and operations.** Costs continue after construction under separate
appropriations, and operations and support fund the ship for its service life. Navy policy governs
the point at which shipbuilding construction funding can no longer be obligated and other
appropriation types must be used.

**Statutory cost cap.** Ford-class ships carry a cost limitation in law, set per hull and amended
several times. CVN-79's cap stood at $11.4 billion at the FY2013 budget position; SECNAV notified
Congress of an increase to $12.936 billion in August 2023 (CVN 78 MSAR, December 2023, which also
reported the ship 91 percent complete). $12.936 billion is the current baseline, not $11.4 billion.
This creates a reported hull-level figure with legal significance whose scope is defined by statute
rather than by the accounting structure, so it does not necessarily reconcile line for line to
appropriation-level execution.

## 2. The reporting artifacts and the named offices

The layer model in `BLUEPRINT.md` section 8 gives producer, purpose, and number characteristic for
each layer. What follows is only the specific artifacts and offices, which that table does not name.

**Acquisition reporting to Congress.** Historically Selected Acquisition Reports under statute, with
the reporting regime and its repository having changed in recent years. The current form and
location for this program needs confirmation. For carriers, cost has frequently been reported at
program or class level rather than per hull, so hull figures often have to be derived rather than
read. See section 6 and the GAO recommendation on this.

**Budget justification material.** The annual exhibits. P-1 lists procurement programs, P-5 carries
cost analysis detail, R-1 and R-2 cover research programs and projects, O-1 covers operations. These
state requested and prior-year amounts in budget structure as of the submission date, and are never
restated afterward.

**SUPSHIP**, the Supervisor of Shipbuilding, Conversion and Repair, is the naval supervisory

# Blueprint: intent, design, and scaling path

Single home for why this exists, what it produces, how it works, and how it grows. Domain facts
live in `BACKGROUND.md`. Decisions already made and gaps still open live in `LOG.md`. Facts are
not repeated across those three files; each points to the one that owns it.

---

# Part I. Intent

## 1. The problem

Nobody can answer "what has CVN-79 cost" with a number that is both defensible and traceable to
evidence. The data exists. What is missing is the connection between how the cost is reported and
how it was recorded.

Four causes:
77ffea5d8049dc37:0001:00.heading: B
legends: # Blueprint: intent, design, and scaling path

77ffea5d8049dc37:0001:01.text:
answer "what has CVN-79 cost" with a number that is both defensible and traceable to
evidence. The data exists. What is missing is the connection between how the cost is reported and
how it was recorded.

Four causes:

1. The cost is reported in several places by several producers, and those places do not agree. A
   congressional report, a budget exhibit, the general ledger, and a contract performance report
   will give different figures for the same hull in the same year. All four can be correct, because
   they measure different things under different scope rules at different times.
2. The accounting record spans multiple general ledger systems across roughly two decades, with
   field definitions and account structures changing at each transition. For this program the
   transition is a hard dated seam rather than a gradual migration. See `BACKGROUND.md` section 3.
3. No one owns the reconciliation between the reported figure and the recorded figure. Each time
   someone needs it, it gets assembled by hand, differently.
4. The scope of "program cost" is undefined in practice. Contract cost is obvious. Whether a
   program office's travel for a site visit belongs in the number is answered inconsistently,
   usually implicitly.

## 2. Why now

scope of "program cost" is undefined in practice. Contract cost is obvious. Whether a
   program office's travel for a site visit belongs in the number is answered inconsistently,
   usually implicitly.

## 2. Why now

**Audit.** The Department is under a clean-opinion mandate, and several active material weaknesses
are this problem at enterprise scale: a reported balance that cannot be traced to supporting
transactions. A program whose cost cannot be walked from report to voucher is that weakness in
miniature. From DCFO, this is the priority that matters most, even where the broader organizational
conversation is framed around AI and budget execution.

**Program cost and independent assessment.** CAPE builds independent cost positions and needs a
traceable actuals baseline. The leadership intent for that handoff is specific: give CAPE a cost
model they can adopt into their own program review and assessment work. That is harder than being
validated once, because a model someone else adopts has to be reproducible without its author, on a
program it was not piloted on.

**AI changes the cost of the work.** The reason this was never done is labor: reading decades of
documents, crosswalking account semantics across system eras, chasing one variance through five
systems. That labor is now compressible, which moves the bottleneck from effort to access and
judgment.

## 3. The goal
legends: # Blueprint: intent, design, and scaling path

## 3. The goal

For a given hull and period, show how the cost appears in each reporting layer, and explain why the
layers differ, with evidence attached to each explanation.

The goal is not a single authoritative number. A single number tied to one declared source of truth
is worth less than a defensible account of how the number is reported, how it is recorded, where
those diverge, and why. The divergence with its cause attached is the product. That is also the
artifact an auditor asks for, which is why audit readiness falls out of the design rather than being
bolted on.

**Success looks like:** a variance table for CVN-79 across available layers where every difference
above a materiality floor has a documented cause or an explicit unexplained flag; a coverage map
stating which layers are accessible and what access would change that; a method a second person can
run on a second hull without the original author; and something a program office, CAPE, or an
auditor can challenge on the merits, because the methodology and its gaps are both visible.

## 4. The design premise: the data is messy and the picture is never complete

Stated before the design because treating this as an exception rather than the normal condition is
how this kind of effort fails.

In a perfect world there would be complete, clean, authoritative data for the whole program history.
There is not, there will not be, and this is the single largest determinant of success. The
architecture is therefore an **investigation apparatus** before it is a reporting apparatus. Its job

This correction matters most, and it explains why the layer numbering kept needing to be fixed.

An earlier version treated the layers as concentric rings, each containing the next, each tying to
the one immediately outside it in a single chain. That kept breaking under review because the data

contract-scoped while the ledger is appropriation-scoped and the contractor's own cost accounting

- **Error.** One figure is wrong. This is a finding, and it goes to whoever owns that layer.

entities even when unreimbursed. The Department implements this in DoD FMR Volume 4 Chapter 19.

`tools/build_corpus_manifest.py` catalogues, `ops/entrypoints/ingest_job.py`

Learned twice against a real workspace, and the second time is the one that

The pattern is the same both times. A catalog and a schema are provisioned

`resources-optional/schemas.yml` holds the seven-schema layout for whoever

The first real deploy failed seven times over with `CATALOG_DOES_NOT_EXIST`,
once per schema. Bundles can define catalogs as of CLI 0.287 with
`engine: direct`, and that is deliberately not what this one does.

In a governed environment, and IL5 is the target, a catalog is created by a
platform administrator against a storage root and a set of grants that are not
this project's to decide. A bundle that owns the catalog either fails there
for want of `CREATE CATALOG`, or succeeds and starts managing a securable the
platform team believes it owns. The schemas are the project's. The catalog is
the environment's.

It would not have worked anyway. On an account using Default Storage, which
this one is, both the REST create and the bundle's own catalog resource fail
with `Metastore storage root URL does not exist` while the UI creates the same
catalog without complaint. `tools/ensure_catalog.py` therefore tries REST,
then `CREATE CATALOG` over SQL on a warehouse, which is the route that does
provision Default Storage, then a `MANAGED LOCATION` if given one. If none
apply it prints what it tried, why each failed, and the catalogs you can
actually use. The deploy script runs it before the bundle and stops there on
failure, because deploying into a missing catalog produces one 404 per schema
and leaves a half-created bundle.

### The index lives in a volume once deployed

Files synced by a bundle are the deployment's own copy, and a job cannot write
back into them. An ingest job writing to `app/data/kb/` in a workspace would
either fail or update a copy the app never reads. So the job writes to
`/Volumes/<catalog>/source/extracted/kb` and the app reads `AIRCARRIER_KB_DIR`.
Unset, it falls back to the index that ships beside it, which is a smaller
index rather than no search.

## The first deploy attempt, and what it found

`databricks bundle validate` failed on all three jobs with *"Missing required
cluster or environment settings"*. The jobs declared `spark_python_task` with
no compute. On serverless, a Python script task must name an environment, and
the bundle fails at validate rather than defaulting to a cluster. Fixed: each
job now carries an `environments:` block and each task an `environment_key`.

The environment version is `var.serverless_env_version`, not a literal in
three places, because IL5 will very likely sit on an older version than
commercial and that has to be a one-line change at transfer. It defaults to
`"4"`. **If validate rejects that value, change the one variable in
`databricks.yml`.** The error names the versions the workspace accepts.
`spec.client` is the older form of the same field and is deprecated.

Two further things that attempt exposed, both now fixed:

Two further things that attempt exposed, both now fixed:

- The CLI is **v1.24.0**. The version check in the deploy script only

# Working log: decisions and gaps

Two append-only registers. **Decisions** are settled questions, so check here before re-opening one.
**Gaps** are open questions, each typed with an executor, so this is a work queue.

Neither register restates the design. Each entry carries the decision or the finding and points to
`BLUEPRINT.md` or `BACKGROUND.md`, which own the full text.

---

# Part I. Decisions

Format: decision, reasoning, supersedes.

**D1. Pilot is CVN-79, and cost history runs from program inception rather than a chosen start
date.** A single hull keeps the layer model testable end to end, and a selected start date would
itself be an undocumented scope decision of the kind this effort exists to surface. Inception is a
stated modeling choice, since contract award, procurement year, and keel laying are all defensible.
See `BACKGROUND.md` section 7.

**D2. Method is funnel and onion-peeling.** Start from reported aggregates, work inward, tie each
layer before trusting the next. The alternative is assembling from transactions upward and hoping a
total emerges, which has no stopping condition and no way to know when the picture is wrong.
Starting from a published figure gives every later step something to disagree with.

**D33. Obligation figures come from the obligation record only, and a press release is never a
record.** A reader-supplied federal extract showed the construction preparation contract had obligated
4,519,300,324 dollars where this effort had carried roughly 1,080,000,000, an understatement by a factor
of four. The earlier figure had been assembled by summing announced Department of Defense contract
modifications. That method cannot produce a contract total for three compounding reasons: daily contract
announcements have a dollar threshold and are silent below it; they omit incremental and installment
funding actions, which are the dominant obligation mechanism on a cost-plus shipbuilding contract and
carry two and a half billion dollars on this one; and they cannot net deobligations, of which this
contract has sixty eight totalling minus sixty seven million. The rule has a corollary that matters more
than the rule. **A large unexplained residual is a finding, not a remainder.** The error was knowable
without any new data, because the residual it created had been written down and then given a narrative
label rather than a test. Two procedural consequences, both now standing.

**D34. Identifier collisions are registered as named hazards with hard exclusions, not left to
reviewer memory.** The hull's construction preparation contract is N00024-09-C-2116. The contract for
the two following hulls is N00024-16-C-2116, and it carries a fourteen point nine billion dollar
modification. Same trailing four digits, seven years apart, three different hulls. Any partial match,
trailing-digit join or fuzzy contract comparison silently merges them, and the merge is undetectable
downstream because every other attribute looks right. The decision is that collisions of this kind go
in the quick-reference key set as explicit exclusions, in the gap register as catalogue work, and in
every query template as a hard filter on full contract number. The general form of the rule: where two
keys differ only in a position a human reads past, the defence is a constraint in the query rather than
a note in the documentation. Opened as G28. See `ring0/RING0_CVN79.md` section N.6b and E-15.

# Delivery plan: sponsor brief and first prototype

Time-bound and disposable, unlike the other four documents. `BLUEPRINT.md`, `BACKGROUND.md`, and
`LOG.md` are durable. This file goes stale on a known date and should be rewritten or deleted after
the brief rather than maintained.

**The commitment.** Initial meeting with the SES sponsor, DCFO, to brief the approach and show an
update. Roughly two weeks out from the 4 November conversation, so the brief lands in the window of
18 to 21 November 2026. Day numbers below count from Monday 9 November.

**What the brief has to accomplish.** One thing: convert sponsor attention into named access. Not
approval of a program, not a budget. A single introduction to NAVSEA 01 or PEO Carriers is worth
more than an enthusiastic reception, because access is the binding constraint and an SES
introduction is the only instrument that moves it.

---

## 2. The event capture design, and the move that makes it approvable

**Capture is a scheduled job writing to a Delta table. The app reads the table. The app never
fetches live.** Three reasons. Provenance: the trust model requires a retrieval timestamp and a
source citation on every item, and a live fetch from the front end records neither. Robustness: a
source being slow or down should not make the demo look broken in front of the sponsor. Governance:
one scheduled job with a narrow allowlist is a far smaller egress request than a front end that
talks to the internet on every page load.

# Transferring to Databricks, step by step

Written for a workspace that has nothing yet. Every step says what it does,
what it needs, and what it looks like when it fails. Run from the repo root.

```powershell
cd C:\Users\Peter-HP\git\AirCarrier\dbrepo
```

---

## Step 0. Prerequisites, once per machine

```powershell
winget install Databricks.DatabricksCLI
pip install databricks-sdk
databricks auth login --host https://dbc-aae0ba16-8727.cloud.databricks.com --profile databricks-dev
databricks current-user me --profile databricks-dev
```

The `databricks` **pip** package is not the CLI and does not give you
`databricks bundle`. Check you have the real one, 0.287 or newer:

```powershell
databricks --version
```

---

## Step 1. Where it lands

The build needs a **catalog and a schema it can write to**. It creates
neither. Both are provisioned objects with storage and grants attached, and
in a governed workspace neither is a deployment's to make. What the build
owns is tables, views, volumes and jobs, all prefixed, all inside a schema
you point it at.

Find one you can write to:

```powershell
python tools\ensure_catalog.py --catalog users --schema <your.name> --profile databricks-dev
```

A personal schema under the `users` catalog is often the only thing a new
user owns outright, and it is enough. Then every later step carries the same
two flags:
9ba5a2b2f4aba2cf:0001:00.heading: T
legends: # Transferring to Databricks, step by step
Copy-Item resources-optional\schemas.yml resources\

9ba5a2b2f4aba2cf:0001:01.text:
users --schema <your.name> --profile databricks-dev
```

A personal schema under the `users` catalog is often the only thing a new
user owns outright, and it is enough. Then every later step carries the same
two flags:

```powershell
.\deploy\Deploy-ToDatabricks.ps1 -Mode Bundle -Catalog users -Schema <your.name> -Execute
```

Everything the build creates is prefixed `aircarrier_`, so it sits beside
whatever else is already in that schema without colliding. Change the prefix
with `-StorePrefix`.

### If you do own a catalog

Create one if you have `CREATE CATALOG`:

```powershell
python tools\ensure_catalog.py --catalog aircarrier --profile databricks-dev
```

It tries REST, then `CREATE CATALOG` over SQL, which is the route that works
on an account using Default Storage where the REST call fails with
`Metastore storage root URL does not exist`. If you have neither, the UI can
still do it: Catalog → Create → Catalog → Default Storage.

With a catalog of your own you can also use the seven-schema layout, which is
the cleaner model because the leads firewall becomes a grant rather than a
naming convention:

```powershell
Copy-Item resources-optional\schemas.yml resources\
```

That needs `CREATE SCHEMA` on the catalog.

---

## Step 2. The bundle: schemas, volumes, jobs, the app

legends: # Transferring to Databricks, step by step
Copy-Item resources-optional\schemas.yml resources\

naming convention:

```

That needs `CREATE SCHEMA` on the catalog.

---

## Step 2. The bundle: schemas, volumes, jobs, the app

```powershell
.\deploy\Deploy-ToDatabricks.ps1 -Mode Bundle              # prints the plan, changes nothing
.\deploy\Deploy-ToDatabricks.ps1 -Mode Bundle -Execute     # applies it
```

Creates two volumes, four jobs and the app definition. No schemas: see Step 1. Three
of the four jobs are paused on purpose: `aircarrier_events` and
`aircarrier_dispatcher` call entry points that still raise
`NotImplementedError`, and `aircarrier_ingest` runs on demand. Only
`aircarrier_tieout` is scheduled, because it is implemented.

This step does **not** move the documents and does **not** start the app.

---

## Step 3. The documents

```powershell
.\deploy\Deploy-ToDatabricks.ps1 -Mode Corpus -Execute
```

Uploads 38MB to `/Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/<prefix>artifacts`, addressed by
sha256, then triggers the ingest job to build the index. Idempotent: each file
is checked by size and skipped if already there, so re-running after a partial
transfer costs nothing.

To see what would move without moving it:

```powershell
python tools\upload_corpus.py --dry-run
```

---

## Step 4. Start the app

```powershell
databricks apps start aircarrier-front-center-dev -p databricks-dev
9ba5a2b2f4aba2cf:0001:02.heading: S
legends: # Transferring to Databricks, step by step
Copy-Item resources-optional\schemas.yml resources\

9ba5a2b2f4aba2cf:0002:00.text:
databricks apps list -p databricks-dev
```

To rebuild the index on its own, without re-uploading:

```powershell
databricks bundle run aircarrier_ingest -t dev -p databricks-dev `
  --var=catalog=users --var=schema=<your.name> --var=store_prefix=aircarrier_
```

`databricks jobs run-now` takes a numeric `JOB_ID` and has no `--job-name`.
`bundle run` takes the resource key out of `databricks.yml`, which is stable
across the job being recreated.

A bundle deploy creates an app. It does not start one. The first start also
provisions a service principal and needs Unity Catalog grants, so budget
calendar time for it rather than minutes.

---

## Step 5. Check it

```powershell
python checks\gates.py --profile databricks-dev
```

Four gates: whether Apps is enabled, what the egress policy allows, whether
the sponsor can open it, whether budget execution is reachable. Read only, and
where a gate needs an admin action it prints the action instead of taking it.

Then open the app URL from `databricks apps list`. The pages to look at first
are `/dashboard`, `/gaps` and `/knowledge`.

---

## All of it in one go

Only once each step has worked separately at least once:

```powershell
.\deploy\Deploy-ToDatabricks.ps1 -Mode All -Execute
```

Order is Preflight → Catalog → Bundle → Corpus → Workspace → Git folder.

| What it says | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `The token '&&' is not a valid statement separator` | PowerShell 5.1 has no `&&` | use `;` or two lines |
| `Metastore storage root URL does not exist` | account uses Default Storage; REST cannot provision it | Step 1 SQL route, or 1a in the UI |
| `CATALOG_DOES_NOT_EXIST`, once per schema | Step 1 was skipped | run Step 1 |
| `does not have CREATE CATALOG on Metastore` | normal in a governed workspace | deploy into a catalog you have: `-Catalog users -Schema <your.name>` |
| `does not have CREATE SCHEMA on Catalog`, seven times | the seven-schema layout is opt-in and you do not have the grant | leave `resources-optional/schemas.yml` where it is; the default layout creates no schemas |
| `unknown field: description` / `expected bool, found string` | a key landed at the wrong indentation in `databricks.yml` | fixed; the line and column in the warning point straight at it |
| `Missing required cluster or environment settings` | a task has no serverless environment | fixed; if it returns, the task is missing `environment_key` |
| environment version rejected | this workspace offers different versions | change `serverless_env_version` in `databricks.yml` to one the error names |

| `Pattern X does not match any files` | a `sync.exclude` entry matches nothing | delete that entry; `.gitignore` is already honoured |
| app starts but search finds nothing | the index is in a volume the app cannot read | check `AIRCARRIER_KB_DIR` in `app/app.yaml` against the real volume path |

## Dropping this into a different Databricks environment

Same five steps. Only three things change, and all three are flags or
variables rather than edits:

1. `--profile`, or `workspace.host` in `databricks.yml` for a new target.
2. `-Catalog`, `-Schema` and `-StorePrefix`.
3. For IL5: the three model service names and `serverless_env_version` in the
   `il5` target, and the adapter selection. `core/adapters/il5/` raises
   `NotImplementedError` from every method by design. That is the transfer
   checklist, written as code that fails loudly rather than as a document that
   goes stale.

Nothing in `ops/` or `app/` should need editing to move environments. If it
does, that is a finding worth recording rather than a patch worth making.

The CVN 78 Gerald R. Ford Class Nuclear Aircraft Carrier (CVN 78) is the successor to the

the war to the enemy through joint multi-mission offensive operations by: (a) being able to

independent of forward-based land facilities, (b) protecting friendly forces from enemy attack 
through the establishment and maintenance of battle space dominance independent of forward-
based land facilities, and (c) engaging in sustained operations in support of the United States 
and its allies independent of forward-based land facilities.      The CVN 78 Class Aircraft Carrier 
program includes major efforts for Nuclear Propulsion/Electric Plant Design, Electromagnetic 
Aircraft Launching System (EMALS) and all electric auxiliary systems.  Additional design

GERALD R. FORD (CVN 78)
CVN 78 departed for her initial operational deployment in May 2023 and, after a two-and-a-half-
month extension following the outbreak of conflict in Israel, returned to her homeport in January 
2024.  While underway, CVN 78 worked with 17 nations throughout its deployment that included 
dual-carrier operations and exercises with navies from France, Greece, Norway, Turkey, and the 
United Kingdom.  During its deployment, the CVN 78 crew conducted 43 underway 
replenishments, logged more than 17,826 flight hours and 10,396 sorties, and sailed more than 
83,476 nautical miles.  With the return of CVN 78 from its initial operational deployment, the 
program continues to execute the class test plan which includes Live Fire Test and Evaluation 
(LFT&E) and Initial Operational Test and Evaluation (IOT&E).  The Total Ship Survivability Trial is 
planned for November 2024 and will be the final test event of the LFT&E program.  With the first 
operational deployment being extended for CVN 78, the IOT&E schedule has been adjusted to 
align with the planned future Composite Training Unit Exercises to demonstrate the Sustained

CVN 79 is 91 percent complete. In August 2023 the Secretary of the Navy notified Congress he 
was increasing the Cost Limitation Baseline for CVN 79 to $12.936 billion. The increase is the 
result of implementing the capability-based ship delivery/post-delivery strategy to move planned 
work from the Post Shakedown Availability (PSA) into the construction period. The Navy 
awarded a contract modification in June 2023 to implement the ship delivery/post-delivery 
strategy and as a result the delivery has been adjusted to July 2025. This approach will prepare 
CVN 79 as the first FORD Class aircraft carrier to operate in the Indo-Pacific region and decrease 
the amount of time CVN 79 would have been required to be at the shipyard after ship delivery to 
conduct the PSA. The revised strategy maintains the overall "ready for deployment workups" 
milestone for CVN 79. In February 2024, the shipbuilder and the crew commenced EMALS dead-
load testing, launching large, wheeled, car-like structures of graduated weights up to 80,000 
pounds to simulate the weight of actual aircraft.

was awarded in October 2022. This CAPEX project installs a new watertight intermediate gate 
lodge to split the dry dock into two sections and enables simultaneous construction of two 
aircraft carriers in the same dry dock. As a result of this CAPEX project, the ability to deliver 
FORD Class aircraft carriers on time is increased by reducing risk in the legacy heel-to-toe 
schedule within the dry dock between the lead and follow-on ship in a two-ship buy. This critical 
public-private partnership agreement established favorable conditions for keeping aircraft

Mission and Description 
The CVN 78 Gerald R. Ford Class Nuclear Aircraft Carrier (CVN 78) is the successor to the NIMITZ Class (CVN 68) aircraft 
carrier. The CVN 78 mission is to provide credible, sustainable, independent forward presence during peacetime without access 
to land bases; operate as the cornerstone of a joint and/or allied maritime expeditionary force in response to crisis; and carry the 
war to the enemy through joint multi-mission offensive operations by: (a) being able to operate and support aircraft in attacks on 
enemy forces ashore, afloat, or submerged independent of forward-based land facilities, (b) protecting friendly forces from enemy 
attack through the establishment and maintenance of battle space dominance independent of forward-based land facilities, and (c) 
engaging in sustained operations in support of the United States and its allies independent of forward-based land facilities. The 
CVN 78 Class Aircraft Carrier program includes major efforts for Nuclear Propulsion/Electric Plant Design, Electromagnetic 
Aircraft Launching System (EMALS) and all electric auxiliary systems. Additional design features and new technologies have 
been added, including a new/enlarged flight deck, improved weapons handling capabilities, and improved survivability.

CVN 78 
 
Program Highlights Since Last Report 
GERALD R. FORD (CVN 78)  
CVN 78 reached Obligation Work Limiting Date in July 2022. The Test and Evaluation Master Plan was signed by Director, 
Operational Test and Evaluation and CVN 78 entered the Initial Operational Test and Evaluation period in September 2022. In 
October 2022 CVN 78 departed its homeport for a service retained deployment and returned to its homeport in November. While 
underway the ship completed more than 1,250 sorties, expended 78 tons of ordnance, and completed 13 underway 
replenishments. In 2023, CVN 78 will depart for her planned operational deployment. 
 
JOHN F. KENNEDY (CVN 79) 
CVN 79 is 89 percent complete. The Navy has transitioned CVN 79 from a two-phase delivery to a single- phase delivery, which 
will deliver the ship from the current construction period with its complete warfare systems and deliver F- 35C capability in 
accordance with the FY 2020 NDAA. The CVN 79 delivery date is being adjusted to July 2025 to support a capability-based ship 
delivery/post-delivery strategy. The Navy is shifting work from the Post-Shakedown Availability (PSA) into the construction 
period to incorporate CVN 78 lessons learned focused on improving the capability of the ship at delivery.

CVN 78 
 
 
Risk and Sensitivity Analysis 
Current Procurement Cost (December - 2022) 
In accordance with Section 121(b) of the Fiscal Year 2019 NDAA (Public Law 115-232), the Secretary of Defense provided a 
detailed certification package in support of the CVN 80/81 two-ship buy Detailed Design and Construction contract to the 
Congressional defense committees on December 31, 2018. The two-ship acquisition strategy resulted in $4 billion in 
procurement savings on CVN 80 and CVN 81 compared to the Navy single-ship estimates. The Navy's projected cost of CVN 80 
and CVN 81, as negotiated with the shipbuilder, and the estimated cost avoidance described in the Department's certification 
package are realistic; informed by a thorough review with the Navy's cost estimating, engineering, and contracting organizations. 
Also, the Department of Defense's Office of CAPE developed an Independent Estimate of Savings for the two- ship procurement 
and forecast savings of $3.1 billion (Then-Year), or approximately 11 percent. The Navy projects $4 billion in savings. The 
primary differences between CAPE and Navy estimates of savings are in Government Furnished Equipment and production 
change orders.

1b96077fc60550c1:0024:01.text:
(Then-Year), or approximately 11 percent. The Navy projects $4 billion in savings. The 
primary differences between CAPE and Navy estimates of savings are in Government Furnished Equipment and production 
change orders. 
Original Baseline Estimate (April - 2004) 
The Cost Analysis Improvement Group (CAIG) and Navy life cycle cost estimates differed by $1.55 billion (FY04) or 5.6%. The 
majority of the delta resides in the production effort. There were three important contributors to the production effort: production 
labor, the hourly billing rates applied to production labor, and the cost of the material to be incorporated in the ship. The 
Research, Development, Test and Evaluation (RDT&E) estimates and Operations and Support (O&S) estimates differences are 
not considered significant.

Mission
The CVN 78 Gerald R. Ford Class Nuclear Aircraft Carrier (CVN 78) is the successor to the 
NIMITZ Class (CVN 68) aircraft carrier.  The CVN 78 mission is to provide credible, sustainable, 
independent forward presence during peacetime without access to land bases; operate as the 
cornerstone of a joint and/or allied maritime expeditionary force in response to crisis; and carry 
the war to the enemy through joint multi-mission offensive operations by: (a) being able to 
operate and support aircraft in attacks on enemy forces ashore, afloat, or submerged 
independent of forward-based land facilities, (b) protecting friendly forces from enemy attack 
through the establishment and maintenance of battle space dominance independent of forward-
based land facilities, and (c) engaging in sustained operations in support of the United States 
and its allies independent of forward-based land facilities.  The CVN 78 Class Aircraft Carrier 
program includes major efforts for Nuclear Propulsion/Electric Plant Design, Electromagnetic 
Aircraft Launching System (EMALS) and all electric auxiliary systems.  Additional design 
features and new technologies have been added, including a new/enlarged flight deck, improved 
weapons handling capabilities, and improved survivability.

USS GERALD R. FORD (CVN 78)
CVN 78 commenced her second operational deployment in June 2025, showcasing advanced 
capabilities across the U.S. European, Southern, and Central Commands. In January 2026, CVN 
78 supported Operation Southern Spear, a mission to dismantle transnational criminal and illicit 
maritime networks.  While operating in the Southern Command area of responsibility CVN 78 
completed a successful four-day sustained Sortie Generation Rate demonstration in February 
2026. The event resulted in the collection of over 40,000 data points to support the modeling 
and simulation of the full 30-day Key Performance Parameter. Following the Sortie Generation 
Rate demonstration the deployment was extended and the ship was directed to the U.S 
European and Central Commands to support Operation Epic Fury. CVN 78's current extension is 
expected to result in an 11-month deployment and break previous records set during the 
Vietnam-era. CVN 78's advanced systems, including the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch 
System (EMALS) and Advanced Arresting Gear (AAG), are designed to deliver greater lethality 
and joint interoperability and are operating as designed while CVN 78 continues with around the 
clock missions in support of Operation Epic Fury.

This file contains Account Breakdown By Award data, which is reported on a quarterly basis from audited agency financial systems as required by the DATA Act of 2014. It is a breakdown of funding for this award by Treasury Account, Budget Function, Object Class, and sometimes Program Activity--effectively linking the appropriation, budget, financial, and award spheres. Financial data is provided at the TAS level for increased granularity, but may easily be rolled up by Federal Account using the federal_account_symbol column. This data is also available from the Custom Account Download section of the site.

Note that the DATA Act of 2014 went into effect FY17Q2; as such, Account Breakdown by Award data is only available from January 2017 onward, and will not be present for award transactions that occurred prior to that point. SECTION 4: CASH MANAGEMENT 
4.1. EARLY RELEASE FROM CASH MANAGEMENT (EARLY PAYMENT).   
a. The Prompt Payment Act of 1997 (Section 3903 of Title 31, United States Code (U.S.C.)), 
requires the Government to make payments in a timely manner:  not early, not late, and requires 
the cash management of invoices (DoD 7000.14-R, “DoD Financial Management Regulations 
(FMRS),” Volume 10, Chapter 7).  Payment must be made 30 days after a valid invoice is 
received, or by the payment date established in the contract.  Otherwise, interest penalties must 
accrue. Public Vouchers are not subject to cas h management.  In addition, the Act requires 
agencies to effectively manage invoices, and allows an agency to make payment up to 7 days 
prior to the required payment date, or earlier, as determined by the agency on a case-by-case 
basis. Implementing regulations are found in Part 1315 of Title 5, Code of Federal Regulations 
(CFR) and FAR 32.9, “Prompt Payment.” 
b. When the application of DoD’s cash management policy for a particular payment impairs 
the performance of a financially vulnerable contractor, the contractor may request the ACO to 
authorize early payment (also known as early release from cash management or waiver of cash 
management).

a94563a9021fbe35:0013:01.text:
r payment impairs 
the performance of a financially vulnerable contractor, the contractor may request the ACO to 
authorize early payment (also known as early release from cash management or waiver of cash 
management). The ACO must promptly review th e contractor’s request to determine if early 
release is warranted and weigh the benefits of making early payment.  DFAS retains final 
approving authority for authorizing early payment. 
c. When the ACO receives a request from the contractor for early release from cash 
management, the following steps must be completed: 
(1) Determine if early release from cash management is appropriate for an individual 
payment. 
(2) Obtain CMO Contracts Director written concurrence prior to submitting the request 
to DFAS. 
(3) Send approved requests for early release from cash management to the cognizant

DFAS Customer Service Branch Chief contact information may be found in the DFAS Order of 
Escalation document, which can be found on the DCMA MOCAS/DFAS Information website.

SECTION 6: PAYMENT WITHHOLDS 
6.1. IMPLEMENTING WITHHOLDS. 
a. In addition to withholding payment for shipments with missing components, some 
contract clauses authorize the ACO to temporarily withhold payment pending completion of 
certain contractual requirements (e.g., subline items not separately priced, technical data) or 
when it is necessary to protect the Government against potential risk of harm.  Since payment 
withholds may not apply to all types of contracts, it is important for the ACO to review the terms 
and conditions of contract clauses and understand the conditions for withholding payment. 
b. Generally, temporary payment withholds are implemented by issuing a withhold decision 
against affected contracts.  The decision must reference the specific contract clause that 
authorizes withholding of payments, indicate the effective date of the withhold, identify 
conditions of the withhold and any specific requirements for the contractor to follow, and 
identify any action required by the DFAS payment office.  The ACO must ensure a copy of the 
withhold decision and related information are made available to the Defense Contract Audit 
Agency (DCAA) for the processing of cost vouchers.  DCAA must be notified with a list of 
contracts and the percentage being withheld in order to apply a withhold.

SECTION 8: PERFORMANCE BASED PAYMENTS (PBP) 
8.1. PBP CONSIDERATIONS. 
a. Definition: Financing payments based upon the achievement of specific, measurable 
events or accomplishments that are defined and valued in advance by the parties to the contract. 
b. PBPs: 
(1) Are a customary method of contract financing. 
(2) Are fully recoverable in the event of default.  
(3) Meet FAR 32.104 requirements for providing contract financing. 
c. PBPs are not: 
(1) Payment for accepted goods or services. 
(2) Payments for partial deliveries. 
(3) Payments based solely on incurrence of costs. 
(4) An incentive arrangement. 
d. A contract (or individual order under an indefinite-delivery contract) can use either 
progress payments or PBPs but not both.  A contract or individual order cannot use progress 
payments for one line item and PBPs for another. However, a contract or individual order can be 
modified to change the contract financing method from progress payments to PBPs, but both 
types cannot be used at the same time. 
e. PBPs can be established on a whole contract or line item basis. When established on a 
line item basis, each PBP event must be associated with a specific line item.

The SR code is used to determine how often a periodic review should be performed.  The

A review date and review completion date cannot be input at the same time.

date based on the SR code. If the review date fi eld is used, enter the specific review date of YY 
MMM DD, e.g., 20 JUN 10, for the next scheduled Progress Payment Review.

9.11. ALTERNATE LIQUIDATION RATES. 
a. Progress payments based on cost create a Liquidation Pool upon payment of the 
Government provided contract financing. When invoices are paid against delivered items under 
the progress payment, the Government recoups the progress payments through the deduction of 
liquidation from the invoice prior to payment.  The ordinary method of liquidation requires that 
the progress payment rate and the liquidation rate must be the same at the beginning of the 
contract per FAR 32.503-8. It is important to note that the liquidation rate is different from the 
progress payment rate. Even though the numerical values of both rates are set equal to each 
other at the time of contract award, each rate has a different purpose, and each rate must affect 
contractor cash flow in different ways.

responsibility. However, in some markets the provision of financing by the buyer is a

Government.

advance payments must not exceed 15 percent of the contract price.

SECTION 12: PAYMENT TERMS INCENTIVE CONTRACTS 
12.1. PROCEDURES FOR COST PLUS INCENTIVE FEE (CPIF) CONTRACTS. 
a. CPIF contracts should include the negotiated target cost, target fee, minimum fee, 
maximum fee, and a fee adjustment formula commonly referred to as a cost share ratio.  If a high 
maximum fee is negotiated, the contract must also provide for a low minimum fee that may be a 
zero or, in rare cases, a negative fee. 
b. The Government must pay the fee to the contractor as specified in the schedule.  
However, when the ACO determines performance or cost indicates that the contractor must not 
achieve target, the Government must pay on the basis of an appropriate lesser fee.  At the same 
time, when the contractor demonstrates that performance or cost clearly indicates that the 
contractor must earn a fee significantly above the target fee, the Government may, at the sole 
discretion of the ACO pay on the basis of an appropriate higher fee (FAR 52.216-10(c)(1)). 
c. Cost Over-Run.

a94563a9021fbe35:0071:01.text:
tes that the 
contractor must earn a fee significantly above the target fee, the Government may, at the sole 
discretion of the ACO pay on the basis of an appropriate higher fee (FAR 52.216-10(c)(1)). 
c. Cost Over-Run. 
In situations where the contractor is experiencing cost growth (e.g., the contractor’s estimate 
at completion or the DCMA independent estimate at completion are above the target cost), the 
ACO should work with the auditor and pricing specialists to use the best estimate at completion 
available to determine the forecast cost over- run.  Furthermore, the ACO should decrease the 
contractor’s target fee amount by applying the Government/contractor cost over-run shared ratio 
stated in the contract.  The share ratio for cost over-run and under-run may be different.  When 
total allowable cost is greater than the range of costs (maximum cost) within which the share 
ratio operates, the contractor is paid the maximum allowable cost authorized, plus the minimum 
fee. 
d. Cost Under-Run. 
In situations where the contractor is experiencing cost reduction below the target cost (i.e., 
the contractor’s estimate at completion or the DCMA independent estimate at completion are 
below the target cost), the ACO should increase the target fee amount by applying the 
Government/contractor cost under-run share ratio stated in the contract.

Government/contractor cost under-run share ratio stated in the contract. When total allowable 
cost is less than the range of costs (minimum cost) within which the share ratio operates, the 
contractor is paid total allowable actual costs, plus the maximum fee in accordance with FAR 
16.405-1. Training on CPIF contracts, examples, a nd tools for determining the impact of cost 
over/under-run on fee can be found on resource page for this manual under the Tools and 
Additional Guidance section.

SECTION 13: VOLUNTARY REFUNDS 
13.1 OVERVIEW.   
A voluntary refund is a payment or credit (adjustment under one or more contracts or 
subcontracts) to the Government from a contractor or subcontractor that is not required by any 
contractual or other legal obligation.  A contract modification, rather than a check, is the 
preferred method for receiving a solicited or unsolicited refund before final payment. 
Modifications should adjust the price for the refund and credit the refund to the applicable 
appropriation in the contract. (DFARS 242.7100 and DFARS PGI 242.7100). 
13.2. PROCEDURES FOR SOLICITING VOLUNTARY REFUNDS OR ACCEPTING 
UNSOLICITED VOLUNTARY REFUNDS. 
Voluntary refunds may be requested during or after contract performance.  Requests for 
voluntary refunds should only be considered after determining that no contractual remedy is 
readily available to recover the amount sought.  If there is no remedy available, proceed as 
follows: 
a. The ACO determines that one or more of the following conditions exists during or after 
contract performance: 
(1) Contractor overcharged under a contract. 
(2) Contractor inadequately compensated the Government for the use of Government-
owned property. 
(3) Contractor inadequately compensated the Government in the disposition of 
contractor inventory.
a94563a9021fbe35:0075:00.heading: UNSOLICITED VOLUNTARY REFUNDS.

a94563a9021fbe35:0075:01.text:
d under a contract. 
(2) Contractor inadequately compensated the Government for the use of Government-
owned property. 
(3) Contractor inadequately compensated the Government in the disposition of 
contractor inventory. 
(4) Retention of the amount in question by the contractor or subcontractor would be 
contrary to good conscience and equity. 
b. The ACO may prepare a package requesting a voluntary refund from a contractor.  Prior 
to issuing a solicitation for a voluntary refund, the ACO must obtain approval from the CMO 
contracts director, command contracts director, and the Executive Director, Contracts (DFARS 
PGI 242.7100(4)). Upon approval,  the ACO must draft a memorandum to General Counsel 
detailing the need to solicit the voluntary refund. 
c. CMO legal counsel must review the ACO’s memorandum, the contract, and related data 
to confirm that there are no readily available contractual remedies and to advise if the proposed 
action would jeopardize or impair the Government’s rights. (DFARS PGI 242.7100(2)).  
d. Upon the completion of the review by CMO legal counsel, the ACO must send the 
voluntary refund request to the contractor. For unsolicited voluntary refunds, the ACO notifies 
the contractor that the Government must accept the refund.

contract type specifies a target cost, a target fee, minimum

contract performance, the fee payable to the contractor is

provides, within limits, for increases in fee above target fee

exceed target costs.  This increase or decrease is intended to 
provide an incentive for the contractor to manage the

1.  Purpose.  Under the authority of references (a) and (b), 
this instruction:  
 
    a.  Establishes the overarching Department of the Navy (DON) 
policy for accountability and management policy of General 
Equipment (GE).  The list of associated references are in 
enclosure (1). 
 
    b.  Assigns roles and responsibilities within the DON for 
accountability and management all DON GE (see enclosure (2)). 
 
    c.  Aligns DON policies for GE with Federal regulations, 
Federal accounting standards, and Department of Defense (DoD) 
and DON policies for property accountability and management. 
 
    d.

(see enclosure (2)). 
 
    c.  Aligns DON policies for GE with Federal regulations, 
Federal accounting standards, and Department of Defense (DoD) 
and DON policies for property accountability and management. 
 
    d.  Provides a framework for financial and physical 
accountability and management of GE to support warfighter 
readiness, financial reporting, and auditability requirements. 
 
    e.  Establishes standard taxonomy for GE (see enclosures (3) 
through (5)).

3.  Applicability 
 
    a.  This instruction applies to the Office of the Secretary 
of the Navy (SECNAV), the Chief of Naval Operations (CNO), the 
Commandant of the Marine Corps (CMC), and all United States Navy 
(USN) and United States Marine Corps (USMC) entities within the 
DON. 
 
    b.  This instruction applies to all GE in the DON.  Detailed 
definitions of GE and the reporting categories can be found in 
the glossary (see enclosure (4)).  
 
    c.  For purposes of this instruction, software that is 
integrated or embedded into GE in order for it to operate is 
considered part of the GE into which it is integrated. 
 
    d.  The physical accountability requirements of this 
instruction shall apply to all property under Capital Leases 
when such property otherwise meets the definition of GE in 
enclosure (4).  In the event of conflicting guidance, financial 
reporting and accounting requirements found in references (c) 
and (d) shall supersede the financial reporting and accounting 
requirements of this instruction for Capital Leases.  For 
purposes of this instruction the entity responsible for 
operating leased property shall be responsible for maintaining 
physical accountability records as required herein. 
 
4.  Policy.

4.  Policy.  This policy governs the accountability and 
management of GE.  It is SECNAV policy to:  
 
    a.  Execute financial and physical management of GE per 
references (b) through (w), including the latest policies, 
procedures, standards and mandates established by the Federal 
Accounting Standards Advisory Board (FASAB), DoD, DON, Federal 
regulation, and the laws that pertain to GE accountability and 
financial requirements.  Specific procedures detailing the 
requirements of this instruction are published in reference (u). 
 
    b.  Require GE management processes and internal controls 
are in place, functioning, are adhered to and tested at all 
levels of command, including DON oversight of shared service 
providers.

    c.  Require DON personnel entrusted with the accountability 
of GE are properly trained regarding the proper use, care, 
physical protection, and financial accounting of GE and are held 
to the highest ethical standards per reference (i).  DON 
personnel entrusted with the management of GE may be held 
financially liable in the event of loss, damage, destruction or 
other unplanned loss. 
 
    d.  Require that Service-level policies for implementing 
accountability and management of GE are in place and reviewed by 
the Service at least every five years.  Initial Service-level 
policies shall be in place or existing policies updated with the 
requirements of this instruction within 12 months following 
signature of this instruction. 
 
    e.  Maximize GE visibility and accountability to support 
sustained auditability and warfighter readiness.  
 
    f.  Require the use of information technology and automated 
information systems, i.e., barcode scanners and Item Unique 
Identification (IUID) where practicable.  Utilize only 
designated automated information systems with standard, common 
processes for procurement and management of GE.

GLOSSARY AND TERMS 
 
1.  Accountability.  The obligation imposed by law, lawful 
order, or regulation, accepted by an organization or person for 
keeping accurate records, to ensure control of property, 
documents, or funds, with or without physical possession.  The 
obligation, in this context, refers to the fiduciary duties, 
responsibilities, and obligations necessary for protecting the 
public interest.  However, it does not necessarily impose 
personal liability upon an organization or person. 
 
2.  Accountability Record/Custodial Record.  A non-financial 
record used to ensure custodial accountability without affecting 
the custodian’s financial reports.  Accountability records are 
used for locally accountable GE, and GE in on loan.  
Accountability records may be maintained in the APSR or another 
suitable system.  Also known as management records. 
 
3.  Accountable Property Officer (APO)/Eligible APO.

r locally accountable GE, and GE in on loan.  
Accountability records may be maintained in the APSR or another 
suitable system.  Also known as management records. 
 
3.  Accountable Property Officer (APO)/Eligible APO.  An 
individual who, based on his or her training, knowledge, and 
experience in property management, accountability, and control 
procedures, is appointed in writing to establish and maintain an 
organization’s accountable property records, systems, or 
financial records, in connection with Government property, 
irrespective of whether the property is in the individual’s 
possession.  APOs are assigned in writing at all levels of the 
chain of command.  The responsibilities of the APO are 
inherently governmental and therefore not assignable to a 
contractor or other non-government entity.  However, contractors 
may perform certain functions in support of the APO.  These 
functions must be mandatory requirements, requiring no personal 
judgment or discretion on the part of the contractor. 
 
4.  Accountable Property System of Record (APSR).  The 
Government system used to manage and control accountable 
property records.  A subset of existing organizational processes 
related to the life cycle management of property; the system 
that is integrated with the core financial system.  The APSR may 
also control and manage accountability records.

25.  Inventory  
 
    a.  The act or process of locating, counting, and reporting 
property.  For DON there are three authorized methods for 
conducting required inventories.  An additional method is 
authorized for interim checks or to supplement required 
inventories: 
 
        (1) By Exception Inventories.  This type of inventory 
uses actions or transactions, e.g., move orders, maintenance 
actions, calibration checks, etc., where the items are “touched” 
by disinterested parties with supporting documentation directly 
associated with an accountable asset. 
 
        (2) Cyclic Inventories.  Also called cycle counting, 
where a portion of the population is counted either daily, 
weekly, or monthly until the entire population has been counted 
within the time period specified. 
 
        (3) Wall-to-Wall.  An inventory process where the entire 
population is counted at a single point in time. 
 
        (4) Statistical Sample.  Sampling does not relieve the 
requirement for triennial or annual inventories but may be used 
to supplement inventory requirements, test, evaluate or validate 
inventory accuracy.

37.  Working Capital Fund (WCF).  A revolving fund (or account) 
that relies on sales revenue rather than direct congressional 
appropriations to finance its operations.  A WCF generates 
revenue by charging customers a stabilized cost recovery rate to 
offset the full costs of its operations, and to finance the 
fund’s continuing operations without fiscal year limitation.  A 
revolving fund is intended to operate on a break-even basis over 
time; that is, it neither makes a profit nor incurs a loss.  
WCFs provide a funding mechanism for DoD and DON corporate 
structures to absorb risk in planning investment programs for 
maintenance and supply.

980db3c2572108aa:0003:00.text:
ABSTRACT 
Difficulties managing cost growth, schedule overruns, and performance issues in 
the Ford-class aircraft carrier program are a critical oversight topic and a key problem 
area in planning for the Navy’s future. While the Navy is conducting research and 
focusing efforts on managing cost growth in production, further research is needed into 
the program management structure and utilization of current acquisition policy and 
guidance to assess possible courses of action. A case study analysis of the 
Ford-class program—contextualized by a review of current literature to include 
acquisition policy—identified the various constraints, priorities, and impacts of 
acquisition strategy decisions to provide insight into future courses of action and 
objectives required for program success. The program has seen poor outcomes, 
primarily due to external pressure and an inability to mitigate constraints despite 
conducting detailed planning for tailored acquisition strategies. Changes are 
recommended to the current utilization of the Major Capability Acquisition pathway 
and organization of program offices and support staff to provide a clearly 
structured framework that mitigates constraints on the design and build process of Ford-
class aircraft carriers.

980db3c2572108aa:0015:00.text:
I. INTRODUCTION
The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) analysis of the Navy’s fiscal year (FY) 
2024 shipbuilding plan describes aircraft carriers as “the heart of the battle force” (Labs, 
2023, p. 37). As the Nimitz class reaches the end of its planned life cycle, the Ford class is 
intended to be a direct replacement by using a Nimitz hull and incorporating new design 
features and improvements (O’Rourke, 2024), as shown in Figure 1. Due to the critical 
importance of aircraft carriers to the Navy, the cost growth, schedule overruns, and 
performance issues surrounding USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN 78) and the follow-on ships in 
the class have become a key oversight topic.  
F
igure 1. USS Harry S. Truman (CVN 75) of the Nimitz class (top) and 
Gerald R. Ford of the Ford class (bottom). Source: Esposito (2020). 
A. PROBLEM STATEMENT
A Congressional Research Service (CRS) report written by Ronald O’Rourke,
updated March 2024, lists the issues that Congress should assess prior to decisions on the 
procurement of future carriers as the carrier force level, program cost growth, deployment

980db3c2572108aa:0016:00.text:
delays, a
nd test and evaluation concerns from the Office of the Director, Operational Test 
and Evaluation (DOT&E). The Navy is conducting various studies to address these 
concerns and determine how the Navy can best achieve necessary operational concepts like 
distributed maritime operations in the future (Office of the Chief of Naval Operations 
[OPNAV], 2023). The FY23 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) additionally 
established a Commission on the Future of the Navy that will independently study the 
Navy’s ship and aviation force structure for Congress (O’Rourke, 2024).  
The Navy’s ability to manage costs in the Ford-class program and deliver the 
desired capabilities will have a direct impact on decision-making related to aircraft carrier 
force levels and the Navy’s overall composition. The O’Rourke oversight reporting (2024) 
identifies that the implementation of various changes to the build and buy strategies for 
future carrier procurement is planned by the Navy to allow for more accurate cost 
estimates, solve identified cost drivers, and improve efficiencies in the construction 
process. However, further research must also examine the program management 
framework utilized for the Ford class and the acquisition strategy decisions that affect the 
management of cost growth and other program issues in execution.

program management framework will allow additional assessment into courses of action 
for the program and provide insights into the D epartment of D efense’s ( DoD) current 
policies related to the acquisition of complex weapons systems. 
B. RESEARCH OBJECTIV ES 
The primary objective of this research is to determine how the Ford class can best 
utilize the adaptive acquisition framework ( AAF) moving forward to maintain the 
acquisition program baseline (APB).  
1. Primary Research Question 
• How can the Ford-class CVN program tailor its acquisition strategies 
moving forward to achieve the program’s required cost, schedule, and 
performance baselines over the full life cycle?

The se
condary research objectives are to study the impacts of acquisition strategy 
decisions over the course of the program so far to assess various courses of action for the 
program moving forward to enable success in both this program and similar acquisitions 
in the future. 
2. Secondary Research Questions 
• What constraints impacted program decisions and how did the program 
prioritize cost, schedule, and performance? 
• How has the program used the principles of incremental development, 
evolutionary acquisition, and modular open systems approach?  
• How have acquisition strategy decisions affected integration of critical 
technology and how do the technologies relate to the Key Performance 
Parameters? 
• How have constraints on the program changed and what acquisition 
strategy updates have been made over the life of the program? 
C. METHODOLOGY 
The primary focus of this research is an examination of the Ford program case 
history as it relates to program decision-making and acquisition strategy changes to 
contextualize the management of the Ford program so far. The case study approach is 
intended to be both a research strategy and a methodology for data collection to be 
descriptive, explanatory, and exploratory in the assessment of the management framework 
being utilized (Priya, 2021).

being utilized (Priya, 2021).  
Using a case study appr oach also enables an assessment of the processes, practices, 
and interactions of the program to enable a root cause analysis of decisions and provide an 
interpretation of the connection between decisions and outcomes (Njie & Asimiran, 2014). 
Finally, an assessment of root causes will enable a discussion of recommendations to 
provide a way forward for program management in the production of future carriers of the 
Ford class.

D. SCOPE AND LI
MITATIONS 
The scope of this research is intended to be a high-level assessment of the 
acquisition strategies and management framework utilized by the Ford class to make 
decisions and provide oversight during program execution. Analysis is limited by the 
availability of information reported in program documents and in assessments conducted 
by other oversight agencies, and the underlying factors behind decisions made throughout 
the course of the program may be hidden due to a lack of in-depth reporting. Program 
recommendations are based on what is allowed within existing policy and guidance. 
E. ORGANIZATION 
This study is organized into five chapters, which provide background and 
contextualize information before presenting an analysis and concluding recommendations. 
• Chapter I provides an introduction of the problems driving this research, 
the research objectives and associated questions, the methodology utilized 
to achieve the end objectives, and the scope and limitations. 
• Chapter II describes the background of the Ford-class program and the 
rationale that forms the specific objectives of this research, as 
differentiated from other studies currently being conducted by the Navy.

• Chapter II describes the background of the Ford-class program and the 
rationale that forms the specific objectives of this research, as 
differentiated from other studies currently being conducted by the Navy. 
• Chapter III provides a review of literature related to acquisition strategies 
and the program management framework to provide context for further 
analysis into the Ford’s case history and an assessment of the way 
forward. 
• Chapter IV provides analysis of the Ford program structure and 
acquisition strategy decision making related to program constraints and 
cost, schedule, and performance priorities. 
• Chapter V provides conclusions based on the current literature, the Ford

maintain baselines over the full life cycle of the class.
